title: Emphysema
subject: Pathology
summary: Permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to terminal bronchioles with wall destruction, leading to loss of elastic recoil and air trapping. In low‑resource settings, smoking, biomass smoke, and alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency are common causes.
aka: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease – emphysematous type

sections.p: Emphysema is defined by irreversible enlargement of alveolar spaces and destruction of their walls, without significant fibrosis. Diagnosis is clinical plus imaging, with high‑resolution CT (HRCT) the gold standard. In settings without CT, a chest X‑ray showing hyperinflation and a spirometry showing a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (<0.70) supports the diagnosis.

t.b: Measures airflow limitation – a reduced FEV1/FVC <0.70 indicates obstruction; a low FEV1 (<50% predicted) suggests severe disease.
Shows hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms, and increased lung volumes; absence of infiltrates helps rule out infection.
Reveals centrilobular or panacinar patterns, mosaic attenuation, and air trapping; confirms diagnosis when available.

sections.p: Severity is staged by the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) using FEV1 % predicted and symptom burden. In low‑resource settings, a simplified staging uses FEV1 % and dyspnoea grade.

t.b: Quantifies airflow limitation; lower values indicate more severe emphysema.
Grades breathlessness from 1 (no dyspnoea) to 5 (too breathless to leave house).

sections.p: The leading causes in East Africa and similar settings are tobacco smoking, indoor biomass smoke exposure, and alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency. Other contributors include chronic infections (TB, HIV), occupational dust, and viral pneumonias.

t.b: Detects deficiency; a level <0.5 g/L suggests disease.
Differentiates reversible obstruction (asthma) from irreversible emphysema.

sections.p: Patients present with progressive dyspnoea on exertion, chronic cough, and wheeze. In advanced disease, barrel chest, pursed‑lip breathing, and cyanosis may appear. Exacerbations are triggered by infections.

t.b: Look for hyperresonance on percussion, reduced breath sounds, and prolonged expiratory phase.
Shows resting SpO2 <90% in severe disease; hypoxia worsens with activity.

sections.p: Investigations aim to confirm airflow limitation, assess severity, and rule out mimics. In low‑resource settings, spirometry and pulse oximetry are essential; chest X‑ray is a useful adjunct.

t.b: FEV1/FVC <0.70 indicates obstruction; FEV1 <50% predicted = severe.
Hyperinflated lungs, flattened diaphragms, and increased retrosternal airspace.
SpO2 <90% at rest or <88% on exertion signals need for supplemental O2.
Level <0.5 g/L confirms deficiency.

sections.p: Urgent red flags include sudden chest pain, severe dyspnoea, haemoptysis, or hypoxia. Complications are pneumothorax, respiratory failure, cor pulmonale, and infections.

t.b: Look for collapsed lung and mediastinal shift.
Oxygen to maintain SpO2 >92%.

sections.p: Management follows a stepwise approach: treat the underlying cause, provide bronchodilators, consider oxygen, and address complications. In low‑resource settings, inhaled short‑acting beta‑agonists and anticholinergics are first line; steroids are used for exacerbations.

t.b: Counselling, nicotine replacement, or varenicline if available.
SABA for acute relief; LABA or anticholinergic for maintenance.
Maintain SpO2 >92%.
Influenza and pneumococcal vaccines.

sections.p: Regular review of spirometry, symptom scores, and adherence is essential. Prevention focuses on avoiding smoke exposure, improving indoor air quality, and early detection of infections.

t.b: Repeat annually or sooner if symptoms worsen.
Annual influenza and 2‑dose pneumococcal series.

sections.p: Emphysema is often mistaken for chronic bronchitis, asthma, or pulmonary tuberculosis. Key distinguishing features are the pattern of airflow limitation, imaging findings, and response to bronchodilators.
b: TB – weight loss, night sweats, cavitation on X‑ray

t.b: Stable FEV1 after bronchodilator indicates irreversible emphysema.

sections.p: Spirometry can be falsely normal in early disease; chest X‑ray may miss centrilobular emphysema. Alpha‑1 antitrypsin levels can be low in acute inflammation, leading to misinterpretation.

t.b: Consider repeat testing if clinical suspicion remains high.
Avoid diagnosing deficiency based on a single low reading during infection.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden chest pain with dyspnoea (possible pneumothorax), severe hypoxia (SpO2 <88%), haemoptysis, or rapid worsening of breathlessness.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of emphysema in East Africa?
faq.a: Tobacco smoking and indoor biomass smoke exposure are the leading causes.
The structural changes are irreversible, but symptoms can be managed and progression slowed.
When resting SpO2 is <90% or <88% on exertion, long‑term oxygen improves survival.

exam: A 45‑year‑old smoker presents with progressive dyspnoea; spirometry shows FEV1 55% predicted and FEV1/FVC 0.65. What is the next best step? — Start inhaled LABA/anticholinergic and advise smoking cessation.
A patient with emphysema develops sudden chest pain and breathlessness. What is the first investigation? — Immediate chest X‑ray to rule out pneumothorax.
When should alpha‑1 antitrypsin testing be considered? — In patients <45 years, with lower‑zone emphysema, or a family history of liver disease.
What is the rationale for using long‑term oxygen in chronic hypoxia? — It improves survival by maintaining SpO2 >92% and reducing cor pulmonale.
Which complication of emphysema is most likely to cause sudden death in a low‑resource setting? — Pneumothorax due to ruptured bleb.
